questions.q: Why must a bar chart's y-axis start at zero?
options: matplotlib refuses to draw bars otherwise
Bars encode value by length, so cutting the baseline distorts the ratio between bars
Zero is the only number that fits on a bar chart axis
Because bar colors depend on the axis minimum
questions.explain: The viewer compares bar lengths. A truncated baseline makes small differences look huge, as in the lesson's South vs West example.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, West spends about 15% more than South. What did the truncated chart (axis from 280 to 330) make it look like?
options: About 15% taller
About the same height
About 15 times taller
About half as tall
questions.explain: South's bar was 3 units tall (283 minus 280) and West's was 45 (325 minus 280), so West looked about 15 times taller.

questions.q: Which chart type may legitimately use a non-zero y-axis range, as long as it is clearly labeled?
options: Bar chart
Stacked bar chart
Pie chart
Line chart
questions.explain: Line charts encode position and slope rather than bar length, so zooming in is acceptable when the axis is labeled.

questions.q: What is the main risk of putting two series on dual y-axes?
options: Choosing the axis ranges can make the series look tightly linked or unrelated without changing any data
Dual axes cannot be drawn in Python
The second axis always has to start at zero
Dual axes double the file size of the chart
questions.explain: Scaling the second axis changes how the lines line up, letting a chart-maker manufacture a story from the same data.

questions.q: A bubble chart scales each circle's radius by the data value. What goes wrong?
options: The circles become squares
The bubbles cannot be colored
Area grows with the square of radius, so a value twice as large looks four times as large
Nothing; radius is always the correct thing to scale
questions.explain: Readers perceive area. Scale area (not radius) by the value, otherwise differences are exaggerated.
